title: Hungry Ghosts PS2 Finally Playable in English
excerpt: Mord of Swoonlight's v1.0 English fan translation of Deep Space's Japan-only PS2 horror Hungry Ghosts is out now — free, in two editions, with 15 endings.
content:
Imagine waking up dead in hell and being told your only way out is to find the Gates of Judgement. Now imagine that game existing for 23 years without ever speaking your language. Well — the gates are finally open.

Hungry Ghosts, Deep Space and Sony Computer Entertainment’s Japan-only PlayStation 2 horror adventure from 2003, has a complete English fan translation at last. Version 1.0 landed on Halloween from Mord of Swoonlight — the real deal, not the Google-translated patch that showed up on r/emulation earlier this year and got called “rough af”.

If you’ve never heard of it, you’re not alone. The game was led by Capcom legend Tokuro Fujiwara, and it’s earned its “hell simulator” nickname honestly: a first-person crawl through the underworld in the spirit of King’s Field and Shadow Tower Abyss. You play a recently deceased warrior fighting Shinigami-like horrors with spear and crossbow, helping lost souls, and chasing one of fifteen endings. Nearly everything you do feeds karma and rebirth systems mixing Buddhist ideas about the afterlife with Western ones — genuinely strange stuff, even by PS2 standards.

The patch is a labour of love a decade in the making. Mord first heard about the game on the Sword of Moonlight forum while helping translate Shadow Tower Abyss, started work around 2012, then lost the project twice to hard drive failures in 2017 before resuming a couple of years later. What’s here now: every line of dialogue, menu, item and journal entry in English, menu graphics redrawn, romaji name entry, plus a companion guide mapping all fifteen endings (spoilers, obviously).

Two editions ship: Standard keeps the original controls; Modern Controls maps movement and strafing to the left stick, looking to the right stick, and attacks to R1. It’s patch-only — you’ll need your own copy of the Japanese disc — free, and tested on PCSX2 2.0 and up. Real hardware is untested, fair warning.

One thing worth saying plainly: the translation itself is human-made. Mord used AI tools only for what he calls “clerical things” — organising spreadsheets, rearranging untranslated portions, spotting duplicate text blocks — and the Sword of Moonlight-hosted version has had the AI-assisted extras (like the widescreen patch) stripped out to meet the site’s GenAI policy. So no, we’re not calling this one AI-free — but the English words on screen are a human’s work, and that’s the part that counts.

One wrinkle: a second, more polished translation from Everdred’s group has been in the works since 2022 — but its translator just left, so its future is up in the air. Mord himself admits that one will be a step up when it lands. Until then, this is the only complete English version of Hungry Ghosts, and after 23 years, that’s reason enough to play it.
